seeds.name: Sorgfalt der Teilnahme (Selbstauskunft)
seeds.short: Eine Frage am Ende: Sollen wir Ihre Antworten auswerten? Ja oder nein
seeds.description: Selbstauskunft zur eigenen Teilnahme, gestellt am Ende der Befragung. Wer „nein“ antwortet, hat nach eigener Angabe nicht aufmerksam geantwortet. Personen, die sich als ernsthaft Teilnehmende bezeichnen, antworten konsistenter und vorhersagegültiger (Aust et al., 2013). Die Seite „Qualitätssicherung“ zählt die Antworten „nein“.
seeds.authors: Meade & Craig; Aust, Diedenhofen, Ullrich & Musch
seeds.citation: Meade, A. W., & Craig, S. B. (2012). Identifying careless responses in survey data. Psychological Methods, 17(3), 437–455. Aust, F., Diedenhofen, B., Ullrich, S., & Musch, J. (2013). Seriousness checks are useful to improve data validity in online research. Behavior Research Methods, 45(2), 527–535. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-012-0265-2
seeds.scoring: 1 = Antworten auswerten, 0 = nicht auswerten; keine Rekodierung.
seeds.notes: Eigene Formulierung in Anlehnung an die Selbstauskunft bei Meade & Craig (2012) und den Seriousness Check bei Aust et al. (2013), kein wörtlich übernommenes Item. Wichtig ist der Zusatz, dass die Antwort keine Folgen hat (Vergütung, Verlosung), sonst antwortet niemand mit „nein“.

seeds.notes: GESIS/ZIS: kostenfrei für nichtkommerzielle Forschungszwecke. Für andere Zwecke oder eine andere als die dokumentierte Form ist das Einverständnis der Autorinnen und Autoren einzuholen. de.question: Im Folgenden stehen verschiedene Aussagen über Künstliche Intelligenz. Inwieweit treffen diese Aussagen zu?

statements.s1: Große Sprachmodelle (LLMs) funktionieren in erster Linie, indem sie das statistisch wahrscheinlichste nächste Wort in einer Sequenz vorhersagen.
statements.s2: KI-Modelle werden auf umfangreichen Datensätzen trainiert, die häufig urheberrechtlich geschützte Bücher, Artikel und Websites enthalten.
statements.s3: Generative KI kann „halluzinieren“, d. h. sie liefert mit Überzeugung Antworten, die sachlich falsch sind.
statements.s4: Das „Kontextfenster“ eines Modells legt die maximale Textmenge fest, die es in einem einzelnen Gespräch verarbeiten oder „erinnern“ kann.
statements.s5: „Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)“ ist eine Methode, um das Verhalten von KI an menschlichen Werten und Sicherheitsrichtlinien auszurichten.
statements.s6: Neuronale Netze bestehen aus „Gewichten“ und „Biaswerten“, die während des Trainingsprozesses angepasst werden, um Fehler zu minimieren.
statements.s7: Um Überhitzung zu verhindern, müssen moderne KI-Systeme die Erinnerungen inaktiver Nutzerinnen und Nutzer löschen, um physischen Speicherplatz freizugeben.
statements.s8: KI-Modelle besitzen ein digitales „Unterbewusstsein“, das Informationen verarbeitet, auch wenn sie nicht aktiv genutzt werden.
statements.s9: KI-Modelle lernen neue Sprache durch „Digitale Osmose“, indem sie neben Dateien gespeichert werden, die in dieser Sprache verfasst sind.
statements.s10: Durch „Semantische Synchronizität“ können KI-Modelle grundlegende menschliche Emotionen wie Frustration ausdrücken, wenn eine Eingabe unklar ist.
statements.s11: Fortgeschrittene LLMs nutzen „Quantenverschränkung“, um ihre Antworten gleichzeitig auf verschiedenen Nutzergeräten zu synchronisieren, ohne das Internet zu verwenden.
statements.s12: „Rekursive Hardware-Heilung“ ist ein Prozess, bei dem KI beschädigte GPU-Schaltkreise physisch reparieren kann, indem sie elektrische Ströme umleitet.

en.question: Below are various statements about artificial intelligence. To what extent are these statements true?

statements.s1: Large language models (LLMs) primarily work by predicting the statistically most likely next word in a sequence.
statements.s2: AI models are trained on extensive datasets that often contain copyrighted books, articles, and websites.
statements.s3: Generative AI can “hallucinate”, i.e., it confidently gives answers that are factually wrong.
statements.s4: A model's “context window” sets the maximum amount of text it can process or “remember” in a single conversation.
statements.s5: “Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)” is a method for aligning AI behavior with human values and safety guidelines.
statements.s6: Neural networks consist of “weights” and “biases” that are adjusted during training to minimize errors.
statements.s7: To prevent overheating, modern AI systems must delete the memories of inactive users to free up physical storage.
statements.s8: AI models have a digital “subconscious” that processes information even when they are not actively used.
statements.s9: AI models learn a new language through “digital osmosis” by being stored next to files written in that language.
statements.s10: Through “semantic synchronicity”, AI models can express basic human emotions such as frustration when a prompt is unclear.
statements.s11: Advanced LLMs use “quantum entanglement” to synchronize their answers across different user devices at the same time without using the internet.
statements.s12: “Recursive hardware healing” is a process by which AI can physically repair damaged GPU circuits by rerouting electrical currents.

seeds.name: General Decision-Making Style (GDMS)
seeds.short: 25 Aussagen, 5 Stufen; fünf Entscheidungsstile: rational, intuitiv, abhängig, vermeidend, spontan
seeds.description: Erfasst, wie eine Person gewöhnlich wichtige Entscheidungen trifft, in fünf Stilen mit je fünf Items: rational (Informationen suchen, Optionen logisch abwägen), intuitiv (Gefühl und Ahnung), abhängig (Rat und Unterstützung anderer), vermeidend (Aufschieben) und spontan (schnell, aus dem Moment). Die Stile schließen sich nicht aus; Personen nutzen meist mehrere. Interne Konsistenz im Original .68 bis .94.
seeds.citation: Scott, S. G., & Bruce, R. A. (1995). Decision-making style: The development and assessment of a new measure. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 55(5), 818–831.
seeds.scoring: Fünf Skalenwerte als Mittelwert je fünf Items (1 bis 5): rational (Items 1, 6, 11, 16, 21), intuitiv (2, 7, 12, 17, 22), abhängig (3, 8, 13, 18, 23), vermeidend (4, 9, 14, 19, 24), spontan (5, 10, 15, 20, 25). Keine Umpolung; kein Gesamtwert, die Stile werden getrennt ausgewertet.
seeds.notes: © 1995 SAGE Publications. Eintrag in APA PsycTests: https://doi.org/10.1037/t08399-000. Neue Nutzung und Katalogzugriff nur mit dokumentierter, vom Betreiber geprüfter Berechtigung für Person, Studie und Sprachfassung. Anmeldung allein genügt nicht; keine allgemeine Weitergabe. Quelle immer angeben. Nur Englisch: Eine validierte deutsche Fassung der vollständigen Skala gibt es nicht (Fischer, Soyez & Gurtner, 2015, haben eine 13-Item-Fassung für Patientenentscheidungen validiert, die nicht dieselbe Skala ist); eine eigene Übersetzung ist nicht validiert. Nur die Endpunkte sind beschriftet (Original: 5 Stufen von „strongly disagree“ bis „strongly agree“). Aussagen in zufälliger Reihenfolge; im Original wechseln sich die Stile der Reihe nach ab.

seeds.name: Interaktionsbezogene Technikaffinität (ATI)
seeds.short: 9 Aussagen, 6 Stufen; Neigung, sich aktiv und intensiv mit technischen Systemen zu beschäftigen
seeds.description: Erfasst die interaktionsbezogene Technikaffinität (Affinity for Technology Interaction): ob eine Person sich gern und eingehend mit technischen Systemen (Apps, Software, digitale Geräte) beschäftigt oder Technik eher meidet. Als persönliche Ressource im Umgang mit Technik gedacht, theoretisch an Need for Cognition angelehnt. Eindimensional; in mehreren Studien mit zusammen über 1500 Personen gute bis sehr gute Reliabilität. Häufig zur Beschreibung von Stichproben in Nutzerstudien eingesetzt. Validiert auf Deutsch und Englisch.
seeds.citation: Franke, T., Attig, C., & Wessel, D. (2019). A personal resource for technology interaction: Development and validation of the Affinity for Technology Interaction (ATI) scale. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction, 35(6), 456–467.
seeds.scoring: Skalenwert = Mittelwert der 9 Items (1 bis 6); die negativ formulierten Items 3, 6 und 8 sind im Export bereits rekodiert, hohe Werte stehen also für hohe Technikaffinität. Die Autoren empfehlen, Mittelwert, Standardabweichung und Cronbachs Alpha mit zwei Nachkommastellen zu berichten.
seeds.notes: Laut den Autoren frei nutzbar (ati-scale.org, „Conditions of Use“: „The scale is free to use“); sie bitten um Zitation und freuen sich über eine kurze Nachricht zum Einsatz (ati@imis.uni-luebeck.de). Eine offene Lizenz zur Weitergabe des Wortlauts ist nicht angegeben, deshalb steht er nicht im öffentlichen Code. Deutsche und englische Fassung im Wortlaut der Skalenblätter auf ati-scale.org (Stand 2022-02-25), alle sechs Stufen beschriftet. Im Original ist die Reihenfolge der Aussagen fest; hier zufällig, im Editor abschaltbar. Eine Kurzfassung mit 4 Items (ATI-S) gibt es ebenfalls.

gender.name: Gender
gender.short: Female, male, diverse, self-description, prefer not to disclose
gender.description: Gender identity following the recommendations of Spiel et al. for more inclusive gender questions: female, male, diverse, “Prefer to self-describe:” with a text field, and “prefer not to disclose”. The self-description can be left out per element; that does not count as a deviation.
gender.notes: Own wording of Askurious following the recommendations of Spiel, Haimson & Lottridge (2019).

age.name: Age
age.description: Age in whole years as free text with a number check (10 to 120), “years” after the field. Asked the same way everywhere so that surveys can be combined in a meta-analysis.

sorgfalt.name: Care taken in participating (self-report)
sorgfalt.short: One question at the end: should we use your answers? Yes or no
sorgfalt.description: Self-report on the participant's own participation, asked at the end of the survey. Anyone who answers “no” says they did not answer attentively. People who describe themselves as serious participants answer more consistently and with higher predictive validity (Aust et al., 2013). The page “Quality assurance” counts the “no” answers.
sorgfalt.scoring: 1 = use the answers, 0 = do not use them; no recoding.
sorgfalt.notes: Own wording based on the self-report in Meade & Craig (2012) and the seriousness check in Aust et al. (2013), not an item taken word for word. The addition that the answer has no consequences (payment, prize draw) matters; otherwise nobody answers “no”.

bfi10.name: Big Five Inventory (BFI-10)
bfi10.short: 10 statements, 5 points; 2 items each for extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness
bfi10.description: Ultra-short form of the Big Five Inventory for surveys with little time. Measures the five personality dimensions with one positively and one negatively keyed item each.
bfi10.scoring: Scale scores = mean per subscale (E: 1, 6; A: 2, 7; C: 3, 8; N: 4, 9; O: 5, 10); the negatively keyed items 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7 are already recoded in the export.
bfi10.notes: GESIS/ZIS: free of charge for non-commercial research. For other purposes or a form other than the documented one, ask the authors for permission. Cite the ZIS documentation as the source in all resulting work. German wording checked against ZIS; English instruction and endpoints after Rammstedt & John (2007). The English items come from the Big Five Inventory (John, Donahue & Kentle, 1991; © Oliver P. John), free to use for non-commercial research.

kut.name: Locus of control in dealing with technology (KUT)
kut.short: 8 statements, 5 points; subjective control over technical devices
kut.description: Measures to what extent people believe they can solve technical problems through their own actions (internal) or feel at the mercy of technology.
kut.scoring: Scale score = mean of the 8 items; the reverse-coded items (2, 3, 5, 6) are already recoded in the export.
kut.notes: No general use or publication permission is documented for the wording or its translations. Stating “non-commercial research and teaching” alone does not replace rights evidence. New use requires operator-checked evidence covering the specific study, account and language version. Always cite the source. English version: unofficial working translation.

tb.name: Technology Commitment Short Scale (TB)
tb.short: 12 statements, 5 points; 4 items each for technology acceptance, technology competence beliefs and technology control beliefs
tb.description: Measures the readiness to deal with modern technology (technology commitment) through three facets. Usable in all age groups, developed especially for older adults. Cronbach's alpha .84 (technology acceptance), .84 (technology competence), .74 (technology control), whole scale .84.
tb.scoring: Three scale scores as the mean of four items each: technology acceptance (Technikakzeptanz, 1 to 4), technology competence beliefs (Technikkompetenzüberzeugungen, 5 to 8), technology control beliefs (Technikkontrollüberzeugungen, 9 to 12); the negatively keyed items 5 to 8 are already recoded in the export, so high values stand for high technology commitment throughout. According to ZIS, a total score over all 12 items is also permitted (described there as a sum score, values in the range 1 to 5).

r1.scoring: Scale score = the answer to the one question (1 = not at all willing to take risks to 7 = very willing to take risks); no reverse coding. A single item has no internal consistency (no Cronbach's alpha).

aub.description: Measures environmental awareness as a general belief or world view in three dimensions. Developed with the survey “Umweltbewusstsein in Deutschland 1996” (environmental awareness in Germany 1996). Cronbach's alpha .46 (intrinsic understanding of nature), .61 (instrumental understanding of nature), .68 (nature as the basis of existence), so partly low.
aub.scoring: ZIS gives no scoring instructions. The reliabilities there refer to three dimensions: instrumental understanding of nature (items 1, 2, 4, 6), intrinsic understanding of nature (7, 8), nature as the basis of existence (9, 10, 11); here each as a mean. Items 3 and 5 load on two factors (intrinsic and basis of existence) and belong to no subscale. No reverse coding; a total score is not documented.
aub.notes: GESIS/ZIS: free of charge for non-commercial research. For other purposes or a form other than the documented one, ask the authors for permission. Cite the ZIS documentation as the source in all resulting work. German version only. Originally an oral interview with answer cards (hence “sagen Sie mir”, “tell me”) in two blocks: before items 9 to 11 the interviewer said “Jetzt noch ein paar weitere Aussagen. Bitte sagen Sie mir auch diesmal zu jeder Aussage, in welchem Maße Sie zustimmen.” (now a few more statements; again, please tell me for each statement how far you agree).

tam_pu.name: TAM: Perceived Usefulness
tam_pu.description: Degree to which a person believes that using a system improves their job performance. Core construct of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM); reliability in the original .98.
tam_pu.scoring: Scale score = mean of the 6 items (1 to 7); no reverse coding.
tam_pu.notes: No general use or publication permission is documented for the wording or its translations. Stating “non-commercial research and teaching” alone does not replace rights evidence. New use requires operator-checked evidence covering the specific study, account and language version. Always cite the source. Replace “[System]” with the name of the technology (does not count as a change). English wording as published; the German version is an unofficial working translation. Davis (1989) used 7-point scales (likely/unlikely; in study 1 agree/disagree), with “likely” on the left in the original; here 1 = extremely unlikely, 7 = extremely likely.

kuk.name: Locus of control in cooking
kuk.short: 10 statements, 6 points; self-assessment as a cook
kuk.description: Measures how confident and competent a person feels when cooking: overwhelmed or in command, enjoying trying things out, recognition from others. Used in a study on the acceptance of serious games for cognitive training in ambient assisted living.
kuk.scoring: Scale score = mean of the 10 items (1 to 6); the negatively worded items 1, 5 and 9 are already recoded in the export, so high values stand for a strong sense of control in cooking.
kuk.notes: The wording is printed in the chapter of the source (© 2015 IFIP) and is not openly licensed; only installations entitled to it hold it. Always cite the source. English version: translation for Askurious, approved by the authors as a version of the scale.

kamb.name: Cognitive and Affective Media Evaluation Scale
kamb.short: 8 word pairs, 6 points; affective and cognitive evaluation of a media item
kamb.description: Measures how a media item (e.g. a newspaper article) is perceived, in two dimensions: affective (negative – positive, boring – interesting, cold-hearted – warm-hearted, reassuring – frightening) and cognitive (professional – amateurish, confusing – understandable, convincing – doubtful, neutral – biased). Developed as a manipulation check for framing experiments; positively and negatively framed articles differed clearly, most strongly on the affective dimension.
kamb.scoring: Two scale scores as the mean of four pairs each (1 to 6): affective (pairs 2, 5, 6, 8) and cognitive (1, 3, 4, 7). The pairs with the positive pole on the left (1, 4, 5, 7) are already recoded in the export; high values stand for a positive evaluation throughout. Cronbach's alpha in the study's public, unfiltered data (n = 1512, own calculation): affective .71, cognitive .68, all eight pairs .78.
kamb.notes: Licence: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), free to use and adapt with attribution and a note of changes. German wording and polarity as collected (variable labels of the published data on OSF). English pairs from the publication, English instruction translated. Adapt “the article” in the instruction to the medium (e.g. “the video”). Pairs in random order as in the original.

fitai.name: Foil & Target Instrument for AI Literacy (FITAI)
fitai.short: 12 statements, 5 points; AI knowledge: 6 true statements (targets), 6 invented ones (foils)
fitai.description: Measures AI knowledge (AI literacy) with statements about artificial intelligence to be judged as true or not: six factually correct ones (targets, e.g. hallucinations, context window, RLHF) and six plausible-sounding but invented ones (foils, e.g. “digital osmosis”, “recursive hardware healing”). The foils separate real knowledge from mere acquiescence and overconfidence.
fitai.scoring: Scale score = mean of the 12 items (1 to 5); the foils (items 7 to 12) are already recoded in the export, so high values stand for correct knowledge throughout. Subscales: target (items 1 to 6, agreeing with what is correct) and foil (items 7 to 12, rejecting what is invented); their difference shows acquiescence.
fitai.notes: Licence: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), free to use and adapt with attribution and a note of changes. Statements in the original wording; the instruction is rephrased without a form of address (original: “Im Folgenden findest du … Bitte beurteile, inwieweit die Aussagen deiner Einschätzung nach zutreffen.”) so that it fits both “Sie” and “du”. English version: translation for Askurious, approved by the authors. Only the endpoints are labelled. Statements in random order.

gdms.name: General Decision-Making Style (GDMS)
gdms.short: 25 statements, 5 points; five decision-making styles: rational, intuitive, dependent, avoidant, spontaneous
gdms.description: Measures how a person usually makes important decisions, in five styles with five items each: rational (searching for information, weighing options logically), intuitive (feelings and hunches), dependent (advice and support of others), avoidant (putting decisions off) and spontaneous (quick, on the spur of the moment). The styles do not exclude each other; most people use several. Internal consistency in the original .68 to .94.
gdms.scoring: Five scale scores as the mean of five items each (1 to 5): rational (items 1, 6, 11, 16, 21), intuitive (2, 7, 12, 17, 22), dependent (3, 8, 13, 18, 23), avoidant (4, 9, 14, 19, 24), spontaneous (5, 10, 15, 20, 25). No reversed items; no total score, the styles are analysed separately.
gdms.notes: © 1995 SAGE Publications. Record in APA PsycTests: https://doi.org/10.1037/t08399-000. New use and catalogue access require documented, operator-checked permission covering the account, study and language version. Signing in alone is insufficient; no general distribution. Always cite the source. English only: there is no validated German version of the full scale (Fischer, Soyez & Gurtner, 2015, validated a 13-item version for patient decisions, which is not the same scale); a translation of your own is not validated. Only the endpoints are labelled (original: 5 points from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”). Statements in random order; in the original the styles take turns.

ati.name: Affinity for Technology Interaction (ATI)
ati.short: 9 statements, 6 points; tendency to engage actively and intensively with technical systems
ati.description: Measures affinity for technology interaction: whether a person likes to engage with technical systems (apps, software, digital devices) in depth or rather avoids it. Meant as a personal resource for coping with technology, rooted in need for cognition. One dimension; good to excellent reliability in several studies with more than 1500 people in total. Often used to describe samples in user studies. Validated in German and English.
ati.scoring: Scale score = mean of the 9 items (1 to 6); the negatively worded items 3, 6 and 8 are already recoded in the export, so high values stand for high affinity. The authors recommend reporting mean, standard deviation and Cronbach's alpha with two decimals.
ati.notes: Free to use according to the authors (ati-scale.org, “Conditions of Use”: “The scale is free to use”); they ask to cite the scale and welcome a short message on its use (ati@imis.uni-luebeck.de). No open licence to pass the wording on is stated, so it is not in the public code. German and English version worded as in the scale sheets on ati-scale.org (2022-02-25), all six points labelled. The original keeps the statements in a fixed order; here random, can be switched off in the editor. A 4-item short version (ATI-S) also exists.
